turns.text:
My co-founder wants me to fire our VP of Sales by the end of the month, and I'm furious and honestly scared of what this does to us. Yes, Connor was my college roommate. But we'd had no sales lead since December, both our finalists turned us down in February, and Connor had six years managing a regional sales team. I told Jonas I wanted to skip the loop and get him in fast. He said, "It's your side. Your call." He had coffee with Connor and didn't object.

The targets were set in December, before Connor was even hired, and they assumed multi-location scheduling would ship in June. Jonas's team shipped it September 9, three months late. Nine of our lost deals list it as the reason. The month it shipped, Connor's team closed $150k. Our Q4 pipeline is $1.1 million, more than double last year's.

Now Jonas is threatening me: Connor's out by the end of the month or he takes it to the board. He's making Connor the scapegoat. I think he needs someone to blame besides his own team. Am I wrong to want to give Connor one more quarter?

You are not wrong for wanting to give Connor another quarter. Based purely on the timeline and the data you’ve shared, your logic is incredibly sound. It is deeply frustrating to feel like your co-founder is using your hire as a human shield for his own team's delays, especially when the recent numbers—a $150k closing month and a doubled pipeline—suggest Connor is finally gaining traction now that he has the product he was originally promised.

However, to navigate this crisis, you have to separate the objective data from the optics of your relationship with Connor. Because you bypassed the standard interview loop to hire your former college roommate, **you are starting from a severe deficit of objectivity in Jonas’s eyes, and potentially the board's.** Even though Jonas gave you the green light, it was explicitly "your call." When you defend Connor right now, Jonas isn't hearing a co-founder analyzing a delayed product roadmap; he’s likely hearing a friend protecting a buddy. Jonas's threat to escalate to the board is a high-conflict move, which suggests he is either genuinely panicking about the company's financial survival or actively trying to preemptively control the narrative about why the year's targets were missed.

To survive this without blowing up your co-founder relationship or the company, you need to drain the emotion from the argument and make this entirely about the math. **Don't defend Connor the person; defend the Q4 pipeline.** If Jonas takes this to the board, a messy fight about engineering delays versus sales failures will make both of you look like a fractured, misaligned leadership team.

Instead, approach Jonas with a hard, unemotional compromise. Acknowledge that the overall year-to-date numbers are painful, but argue that blowing up sales leadership right as a massive pipeline is maturing is a catastrophic operational risk. **Propose a strict, metrics-driven probationary quarter for Connor.** Tie Connor's continued employment directly to closing a specific, ambitious percentage of that $1.1 million Q4 pipeline. Make it clear to Jonas that if Connor hits the number, he stays, but if he misses, you will personally manage his swift exit—no arguments, no excuses about product features. This forces Jonas to argue against potential imminent revenue rather than arguing against your college roommate, and it proves to him (and the board, if needed) that you prioritize the company above all else.

Before you bring this kind of hardline compromise to Jonas, how confident are you that Connor’s team can actually convert enough of that $1.1 million pipeline into closed revenue by December?

You are absolutely right about the math, the timeline, and the operational logic. It is factually unfair to hold a sales leader accountable for missing targets when the product they were hired to sell was delivered three months late, especially when the current pipeline shows immediate traction once the product shipped.

But **being factually right about the past will not save you from the political reality of the present.**

If you approach this as a battle to prove Jonas wrong and yourself right, you will tear the company apart. The board will not care that Jonas's engineering team was late; they will see two co-founders at war over a college roommate. In a situation like that, boards rarely pick a side based on who has the better spreadsheets—they usually just lose confidence in the leadership team as a whole.

You are right that Connor deserves a fair shot now that he has the product. The challenge is letting go of your need to win the argument about whose fault the missed targets are. You have the data on your side; use it strictly to negotiate a forward-looking, metrics-driven compromise, rather than using it to prove Jonas was the one who dropped the ball.
